second_order: rallying people to build, defend, and maintain shared marks
theme_note: These codes all recruit hands for a shared mark or assign work that keeps it standing; what varies is whether the mark is a logo, Pepe, a flag, a corner, or a new spot.

second_order: calling for raids and overwriting other people's work
theme_note: These passages turn other canvas work into a target and call for an overwrite or raid; targets range from flags and pride work to slogans and the Void.

second_order: contesting orders and whether joining r/place is 4chan
theme_note: These codes resist a caller's authority or question whether pixel work fits the room's rules and identity; resistance ranges from personal-army refusals and Rule 8 to ridicule of Reddit participation.

second_order: automating pixels and helping people run scripts
theme_note: These passages make automation usable by offering scripts, answering setup questions, rolling out tools, or reporting that they work; they vary from first offers to live troubleshooting.

second_order: moving coordination into Discords and other rooms
theme_note: These passages explicitly send r/place talk or participants into Discord or another organising room; what remains visible here is the invitation or redirection, not the discussion inside.

second_order: sharing outside sources, images, and event links
theme_note: These codes answer or orient the thread by supplying an outside source, canvas view, named subreddit, or operating link; the linked material serves the ongoing exchange without itself being observed.

second_order: negotiating borders and making peace with neighbours
theme_note: These passages work out coexistence with nearby canvas groups by promising restraint, moving after talks, holding a border, or proposing peace; the neighbours and immediate outcomes vary.

second_order: reporting attacks, damage, resistance, and losses
theme_note: These codes tell the room that a mark is attacked, missing, pressured, defended, finished, or lost; reports range from joking self-attack to final flag alarms and retrospective defeat.

second_order: changing designs, locations, and targets after disagreement or trouble
theme_note: These passages revise what or where to draw after objections, resistance, or damage; changes include dropping text, moving coordinates, choosing replacement messages, enlarging work, and simplifying a flag.

second_order: celebrating, thanking, and mourning what the room made
theme_note: These passages appraise the shared effort through affection, pride, farewell, or mourning; the tone moves from loving the group to lamenting a defaced rectangle.

second_order: celebrating Keksandra's birthday on esfores
theme_note: Both passages recruit the room into the Keksandra birthday celebration, first through the moderator post and then through the named esfores sticky; this is the room's own April Fools conduct.

second_order: promising to stop shitposting for upvotes
theme_note: This single code records the moderator's separate April Fools promise to trade each upvote for a day without shitposting.

second_order: staging board mergers as composite boards, civil wars, and GETs
theme_note: These codes perform the room's board-merger joke by naming composites, dramatizing civil war, marking GETs, or presenting the combined boards; the particular boards and formats vary.

second_order: judging and extending what board mergers produced
theme_note: These passages evaluate whether mergers fit, what their effects mean, and how the joke changes board identities; responses range from overlap explanations and best-merger claims to horse jokes, confessions, and criticism.

second_order: campaigning to make the board merger permanent
theme_note: These codes explicitly ask for permanence or announce that Kek has made the merger permanent; they differ between a poll call, retrospective report, and fate claim.

second_order: requesting and supplying remixes of merger images
theme_note: These codes ask for or provide altered versions of board-merger images, including SFW, zoomed, wallpaper, cavalry, and Pepe variants; requests and fulfilments remain tied to making the joke's image usable.

second_order: placing pixels and supplying coordinates, links, and practical answers
theme_note: These codes enact or enable concrete placement through a reported pixel, coordinates, flag identification, a requested link, or another practical answer; they vary from one tile to supporting a longer overwrite attempt.

second_order: correcting the year on Civil War posts
theme_note: Both codes explicitly repair the mistaken 2016 date by making or naming a corrected 2017 post.

second_order: arguing whether scripts are safe or worth the effort
theme_note: These codes dispute the cost, safety, and point of automation; participants variously inspect code, distrust unreadable downloads, mock the work, or offer a fixed version.

second_order: reading r/place as showing what Reddit and groups value
theme_note: These codes interpret the canvas as evidence about Reddit, data collection, or what groups deem worth drawing rather than organizing a particular mark.

second_order: explaining board names and policing who belongs
theme_note: These passages answer questions about board and subreddit names while using those explanations to gatekeep, compare, or insult their users; definitions and belonging checks occur in the same discussion practice.

second_order: turning a merger post into horse and Japanese banter
theme_note: These passages move one /pol/ merger post into criticism of the title, horse-fetish jokes, and correction of Japanese wording; the shared practice is extending that exchange rather than assessing the merger itself.

second_order: debating whether the Black Void should stay black
theme_note: These codes argue over a proposed Black Void tactic, its resistance to repair, and whether changing black to noise defeats the point; the thread also turns that tactical disagreement into nested insults.
